Contactless electroreflectance (CER) spectroscopy was used to study GaN/(Ga,Mn)N structures with Mn concentrations ranging from 0.1% to 7%.
The Fermi level in (Ga,Mn)N with x > 0.1% Mn was found to be located approximately 1.25 - 1.55 eV above the valence band edge.
The Fermi level position was independent of the GaN cap thickness, indicating it is predominantly determined by the bulk properties of the (Ga,Mn)N layer.
The band gap change in (Ga,Mn)N was estimated to predominantly take place in the valence band, with a valence band offset of -0.028 ± 0.008 eV per % Mn.
The strong Fermi level pinning, negligible surface depletion layer, and high resistivity of (Ga,Mn)N make it a promising insulating buffer material for nitride devices.
The samples were grown by molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) and characterized using X-ray diffraction, secondary ion mass spectrometry, and superconducting quantum interference device magnetometry.
The GaN/(Ga,Mn)N structures consisted of a (Ga,Mn)N layer capped with an undoped GaN layer, with the GaN cap thickness varying from 31 to 170 nm.
The presence of Franz-Keldysh oscillations in the CER spectra confirmed the sensitivity of the method to the built-in electric field in the GaN cap layer.
The strength of the built-in electric field in the GaN cap layer was used to determine the Fermi level position in the underlying (Ga,Mn)N layer.
For low Mn concentrations (x < 0.1%), the Fermi level was found to be closer to the conduction band, similar to the position at the GaN surface.
The Fermi level pinning and negligible surface depletion in (Ga,Mn)N indicate its potential as an insulating buffer material for GaN-based devices.
The results provide the first estimation of the Mn-related band offsets between GaN and (Ga,Mn)N.
The strong mid-gap Fermi level pinning and insulating properties of (Ga,Mn)N make it a promising alternative to Fe or C doped GaN as a buffer layer in GaN-based devices.
The CER technique allowed the Fermi level position and band offsets to be determined independently of the electrical properties of the (Ga,Mn)N layers.
The findings support the superexchange Mn3+-Mn3+ coupling scenario proposed to explain the low-temperature ferromagnetism in (Ga,Mn)N.
